land.text: Allada, conquered by Dahomey in March 1724; 'Dahomey permitted the existence of a subordinate royalty'

successors.note: The page's rulers table has Dè-Houffon-Agonmin ruling under Dahomey March 1724-1742; 'In 1894, France re-established the kingdom under its control'; annexed by France in 1904 yet allowed to continue; the title of king re-established in 1992.

capitals.name: Allada
capitals.note: Approximate coordinates: the page names Allada as the capital ('the city of Allada had a population of approximately 30,000 people' by the mid-15th century) and gives no coordinates.

correction.text: the Aja kingdom of Allada before the split of c. 1600, including the plateau of Abomey and Ajashe (Porto-Novo) later settled by the brothers

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe. 'in the 12th or 13th century' Aja migrants from Tado founded the city and kingdom; the infobox gives '12th/13th century-1724'; 'The state reached the peak of its power in the 16th and early 17th centuries'. The page gives no area or frontier; Atlantique without a 40 km circle round Ouidah (Whydah, a separate kingdom from c. 1580 on the Whydah page), plus the two seed sites, stands for it; confidence low.

correction.text: Allada after the three brothers split the rule c. 1600: Allada alone

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe. 'until c. 1600, when three brothers - Kokpon, Do-Aklin, and Te-Agdanlin - split the rule of the region amongst themselves' (Allada kept; Dahomey and Porto-Novo are the others). Peak slave sales 'about 55,000 during the 1680s'.

region.text: the city and kingdom of Allada

ledger.note: 12th or 13th century: Aja migrants from Tado found Allada. 'in the 12th or 13th century' (lead); infobox '12th/13th century-1724'; the page gives no year.

c. 1600: the brothers split the Aja kingdom. 'until c. 1600, when three brothers - Kokpon, Do-Aklin, and Te-Agdanlin - split the rule of the region amongst themselves'; Do-Aklin founds Dahomey on the Abomey Plateau (Dahomey page: 'established around 1600 as an offshoot of the royal dynasty of the Kingdom of Allada').
c. 1600: Te-Agdanlin's share becomes Little Ardra / Ajatche (Porto-Novo). The Porto-Novo page has Te-Agbalin's group reach the region of Ajashe 'in the late 16th century'.

1724 (March): Dahomey invades Allada. 'In 1724, Dahomey invaded Allada; in three days, the King of Dahomey's troops slaughtered thousands' (the Agaja page: 'On March 30, 1724, Agaja's army entered Allada').
1724 (March): Allada falls. 'more than 8,000 of Allada's population (mostly Aja people) were captured and sold into slavery'; De Adjara reigned to March 1724.
1724 (March): Allada passes to Dahomey. 'Following Dahomey's subjugation of the kingdom, in 1724, Dahomey permitted the existence of a subordinate royalty.'
1724 (March): the independent Kingdom of Allada ends. Dè-Houffon-Agonmin ruled under Dahomey, March 1724-1742.

wars.name: Dahomean conquest of Allada
wars.outcome: Dahomey won in March 1724: thousands slaughtered in three days, more than 8,000 captured and sold; a subordinate royalty allowed.
wars.note: The Agaja page (opened for the Dahomey dossier) dates the entry of Agaja's army to 30 March 1724.

certainty.note: No page gives a frontier; the shape is the Atlantique department less Whydah, a stand-in.

notes: The Kingdom of Allada has no Cliopatria row. The Wikipedia article is titled 'Kingdom of Ardra'; the slug follows the name used by the Dahomey and Akwamu dossiers of this batch (kingdom-of-allada). Pages: Ardra (main), Porto-Novo, Dahomey and Agaja (shared). The page gives no area, no capital coordinates (the dot is approximate), no frontier and no date for the founding. Whydah: the Whydah page says it 'became independent in the late 17th century' and gives a timeline 'c. 1580-1728' without naming Allada, so the Whydah coast (a 40 km circle round Ouidah) is left out of the Allada shapes throughout. The brothers' split is dated c. 1600 by the Allada page; the Dahomey page's 1600 founding agrees.
